facts.text: Scotia began as a company town called Forestville in 1863, built by the Pacific Lumber Company to house its redwood workers.
In 1888 the town was renamed Scotia to avoid confusion with another Forestville, a change that reflected its many New Brunswick and Nova Scotia residents.
A railroad built in 1885 linked Scotia to the Humboldt Bay and Eel River lines, eventually becoming part of the national network by 1914.
The Scotia Museum preserves the town’s history, showcasing photographs from the Neill Photo Album that document daily life from 1908 to 1913.
Julia “Butterfly” Hill spent two years living in the ancient redwood Luna, a gesture that helped protect the tree from being cut down.
After Pacific Lumber declared bankruptcy in 2008, Scotia transitioned from a wholly company-owned town to a community where former workers can buy and sell individual homes.
